addressed_problems.content: The study evaluated deepfake detection models at the frame level using FaceForensics++, which extracts individual frames from videos, thereby not capturing temporal dynamics inherent to video deepfakes. It remains an open problem to develop pruning strategies that operate on temporal features (e.g., using architectures that model inter-frame inconsistencies) and to evaluate whether winning tickets can be identified in such temporally informed architectures, which would be necessary for efficient video-level deepfake detection.

The pruning criteria used in this work—global and local magnitude thresholds—were not specifically designed to preserve manipulation artifacts. It is unresolved how alternative importance measures, such as gradient-based saliency, feature-frequency importance, or artifact-aware metrics, affect the retention of rare but critical features for deepfake detection. Exploring these criteria could lead to pruning methods that better maintain sensitivity to subtle forgery cues.

The iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) procedure requires eight rounds of retraining, incurring substantial computational overhead that limits real-time applicability. Designing efficient retraining strategies or methods that directly discover winning tickets without full iterative training is an open engineering challenge, and addressing it would facilitate deployment of pruned deepfake detectors in resource-constrained environments.

The study fixed the per-iteration pruning rate at 20% of weights. The sensitivity of winning ticket discovery to smaller pruning steps (e.g., 5–10% per iteration) has not been quantified for deepfake detection tasks. Investigating this sensitivity is important because prior research suggests that finer granularity may better preserve rare features, and could impact the optimal sparsity-performance trade-off.

The study compared IMP only against one-shot magnitude pruning. The effectiveness of other one-shot selection methods—such as SNIP, GraSP, or layer-wise saliency pruning—for identifying winning tickets in deepfake detection models remains unquantified. Evaluating these methods could provide lower-cost alternatives to IMP while maintaining feature retention.

The relationship between network sparsity and robustness to adversarial attacks has not been studied in the context of deepfake detection. It is an open question whether pruned subnetworks are more or less vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, and how pruning affects detection reliability under attack. Understanding this relationship is critical for deploying robust sparse detectors.

While the study demonstrated transferability of winning tickets across datasets (OpenForensic and FaceForensics++), it has not been tested across different deepfake generation methods. Whether the discovered critical features generalize to synthetic media produced by diverse generative models remains an open scientific question, with implications for developing universal sparse detectors.

Deepfake detection requires models that can reliably distinguish synthetically manipulated facial images and video frames from authentic content, yet the prior state of knowledge left two intertwined gaps that motivate this work. First, existing deepfake detectors—ranging from lightweight, mesoscopic networks to deep residual and separable-convolution architectures—are typically treated as black boxes: their internal feature learning mechanisms (which image regions and which frequency/temporal cues they rely on) are poorly understood, so it is unclear which features are essential for reliable detection. Second, practical deployment of detectors is constrained by model size and computational cost: although the neural network compression literature shows that standard image-classification models possess large redundancies (allowing aggressive pruning), it was unknown whether the same sparsity patterns, pruning algorithms, and pruning granularity would preserve the rare, subtle manipulation artifacts that deepfake detection must capture. Prior work used global magnitude pruning and one-shot schemes or specialized detection architectures, but these approaches either (a) applied pruning without analyzing bias against infrequent but critical features, (b) relied on dense overparameterized networks impractical for resource-limited settings, or (c) evaluated detectors on datasets with differing compression and manipulation types without characterizing dataset-dependent pruning behavior. As a result, researchers lacked (i) quantitative evidence about whether “winning-ticket” subnetworks exist for deepfake detectors, (ii) principled comparisons of iterative versus one-shot pruning in the deepfake setting, (iii) insight into how pruning changes model attention (semantic regions versus high-frequency or temporal artifacts), and (iv) knowledge about whether sparse subnetworks discovered on a large dataset transfer to smaller or more compressed datasets. These gaps prevented confident development of compact, interpretable, and transferable deepfake detectors suitable for deployment and limited understanding of which features and pruning strategies are appropriate for this problem domain.

nodes.content: Detecting deepfakes in resource-constrained environments demands compact models that still capture the manipulation cues used by larger networks. Prior approaches either used the full MesoNet dense model or applied coarse pruning without quantifying how much accuracy is lost at extreme sparsity on large clean image datasets. Without concrete per-architecture, per-dataset measurements, practitioners could not judge whether very small models (on the order of thousands of parameters) could still detect deepfakes reliably. Showing that MesoNet preserves nearly 90% of its dense accuracy at 80% sparsity on OpenForensic provides the missing quantitative assessment needed to evaluate MesoNet’s suitability for low-resource deployment and clarifies the extent to which compact mesoscopic architectures can retain critical manipulation-sensitive features.

Prior compression results in standard vision tasks suggested that large models contain substantial redundant weights, but it was unclear whether deepfake detectors—whose discriminative cues may be subtle and localized—would exhibit similar redundancy. Without concrete per-architecture empirical comparisons, there was no basis to select architectures that could be aggressively compressed without sacrificing detection accuracy. Demonstrating that CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet each retain essentially their full accuracy at 80% sparsity on a large, relatively clean dataset addresses this gap by providing precise benchmarks that show which architectures are robust to compression and by how much, informing architecture choice for compact detection systems.

Deepfake datasets differ in compression, generation artifacts, and temporal content; pruning strategies that ignore layer-specific importance risk discarding delicate, layer-localized features needed to detect compressed forgeries. Previous studies often applied global pruning or one-shot schemes without resolving whether local control per layer matters for datasets with heavy compression and dataset-specific artifacts. Establishing that ResNet-18 performs substantially better under local pruning on FaceForensics++ provides the dataset-specific evidence necessary to choose pruning strategies that preserve manipulation-sensitive features in compressed-video-derived datasets.

One-shot magnitude pruning is computationally cheap but lacks iterative refinement and may discard fragile, rare manipulation features. Applying IMP requires concrete operational choices (round count $J$, per-iteration pruning fraction, global versus local thresholding, whether to prune Conv and MLP layers uniformly, optimizer and learning rate, and stopping criteria). Prior to this work, these choices were not explicitly validated for deepfake detection tasks. Providing a full, reproducible IMP configuration (including the mask update formula and the experimental schedule) fills this methodological gap by specifying how to search for winning-ticket subnetworks in the context of deepfake detection and by enabling controlled comparisons between iterative and one-shot approaches.

One-shot pruning is attractive for its computational efficiency, but prior evidence suggested iterative methods can better preserve trainability and performance in vision models. For deepfake detection—where discriminative cues can be rare and subtle—it was unknown whether iterative pruning would consistently yield measurable gains over one-shot approaches, and whether those gains would matter at extreme sparsity levels relevant to deployment. Demonstrating IMP’s superior preservation of accuracy, especially when using layer-aware thresholds, resolves this methodological uncertainty and recommends iterative schemes for practitioners prioritizing accuracy at high compression.

Pruning algorithms are often evaluated on standard classification datasets; however, deepfake datasets vary in how compression and generation methods distribute discriminative cues across layers and frequencies. Without dataset-aware analysis, applying a single pruning policy (e.g., global magnitude) risks discarding layer-local features crucial for detecting compressed forgeries. Characterizing the dataset-dependent trade-off between global and local pruning provides the necessary guidance to select pruning rules that align with the statistical structure of the target dataset and the fragility of the discriminative cues it contains.

Understanding whether pruning preserves the model’s focus on the physically meaningful or semantically interpretable regions (versus forcing the model to rely on spurious or non-human-interpretable cues) is essential for interpretability and trust. Before this study, it was unclear whether extreme parameter reduction would destroy the network’s ability to attend to the same facial regions that dense detectors use, or whether pruning would shift attention unpredictably. Showing that attention remains localized but tighter, and that pruned networks rely more on high-frequency and temporal cues, clarifies the types of features robust to pruning and explains why extreme sparsity can eventually harm performance by narrowing the spatial coverage of attention.

Transferability of compressed models is critical for real-world deployment where collecting large, labeled deepfake datasets for every target domain is infeasible. Prior to this work, evidence that low-parameter winning tickets found on one dataset would preserve detection performance when transferred to datasets with different compression and generation characteristics was limited. Providing concrete cross-dataset transfer accuracies quantifies how much performance can be expected when reusing sparse subnetworks, enabling more informed decisions about training and deployment workflows in constrained settings.

Model selection for lightweight, deployable detectors requires knowing whether to begin with a compact base network or a larger overparameterized model intended for later pruning. Before this work, it was unclear which strategy yields the best compact detector under strict parameter budgets. Clarifying that larger models can produce robust sparse subnetworks (while compact models are brittle) informs the design pipeline: training a larger model and extracting a winning ticket can be preferable to training an already compact architecture that cannot be pruned further without losing crucial features.

One-shot pruning is attractive for speed, but for transferability it may discard weights whose importance only becomes evident after retraining iterations. Without measurements comparing transfer performance between iterative and one-shot methods, practitioners could erroneously choose one-shot pruning and suffer degraded generalization when applying subnetworks to new datasets. Demonstrating IMP’s superior cross-dataset transfer performance addresses this methodological uncertainty and supports iterative pruning when transferability is a goal.

MesoNet, pruned using Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with global thresholds (20% weight removal per iteration for 8 rounds, applied uniformly across convolutional and MLP layers, Adam optimizer with learning rate $1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping patience 10), achieves 56.2% test accuracy at 80% sparsity on the OpenForensic dataset, using approximately 3,000 parameters (0.003M). This accuracy corresponds to 89.8% of the dense model's baseline accuracy (62.6%), demonstrating that a highly compressed MesoNet subnetwork preserves most of the original detection performance on this dataset.

metadata.narrative: The quantitative layer of this conclusion is undermined by P1: the single-run accuracy (56.2%) lacks error bars, making the specific retention of 89.8% unreliable. The qualitative direction (substantial performance at 80% sparsity) is more credible due to H1, which shows that the evaluation was conducted consistently across multiple architectures and datasets. However, the estimate of "substantial" cannot be precisely bounded. The conclusion's core empirical claim is plausible but not statistically robust.

nodes.title: MesoNet achieves 56.2% test accuracy at 80% sparsity on OpenForensic via IMP with global thresholds

nodes.content: For CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet on the OpenForensic dataset, Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with global thresholds (20% weight removal per iteration for 8 rounds, uniformly across layers, Adam lr=$1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping patience 10) yields 80%-sparsity test accuracies of 90.88% (99.4% of the dense baseline 91.41%), 94.29% (99.9% of the dense baseline 94.3%), and 96.11% (99.9% of the dense baseline 96.20%), respectively. Thus, at 80% sparsity on this dataset, these architectures contain sparse subnetworks that preserve almost all original performance.

metadata.narrative: P2 identifies that the near-perfect retention values (99.4%–99.9%) come from single-run estimates and that the tiny difference for ResNet-18 (0.01%) is within typical noise. Without uncertainty quantification, the precise percentages are not reliable, though the qualitative pattern of very high retention across three architectures is supported. H1 reinforces the cross-architecture consistency. The conclusion that these architectures maintain near-baseline accuracy at 80% sparsity is likely correct, but the exact retention margins (99.4%, 99.9%) should not be treated as precise.

nodes.title: CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet maintain near-baseline accuracy at 80% sparsity on OpenForensic via IMP with global thresholds

nodes.content: For the FaceForensics++ dataset (a dataset of 11,600 training images from face-cropped frames of 400 videos with varied compression and deepfake generation artifacts), ResNet-18 pruned with Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) using local (per-layer) thresholds (20% weight removal per iteration for 8 rounds, Adam lr=$1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping patience 10) retains 83% test accuracy at 80% sparsity, outperforming both its dense baseline and the same network pruned using global thresholds. Thus, local pruning yields superior preservation of critical layer-specific features on compressed, challenging datasets.

metadata.narrative: P3 reveals a direct internal contradiction: the conclusion claims that local pruning at 80% sparsity "outperforms" the dense baseline, but the paper's own data (Table I) shows the dense baseline at 85.3% and the pruned model at 83%. This invalidates the "outperforming baseline" part of the conclusion. The subclaim that local pruning outperforms global pruning on FaceForensics++ may still hold, but it is not isolated from the contradiction. H1 provides some support for the empirical pattern across architectures, but it does not resolve the data conflict. Overall, the conclusion as stated is partially false; the credible portion is that local pruning preserves a large fraction of baseline performance (but not exceeding it).

nodes.title: ResNet-18 achieves 83% accuracy at 80% sparsity on FaceForensics++ with IMP-local, outperforming dense baseline and IMP-global

nodes.content:
Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) for deepfake detection is implemented as follows: initialize binary mask $\mathbf{m}^{(0)} = \mathbf{1}$; for each pruning round $j=1,\dots,J$ (with $J=8$ rounds) train the network $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{m}^{(j-1)} \odot \theta^{(j-1)})$ for one cycle, compute a pruning threshold $\alpha^{(j)}$, and update the mask per-global or per-layer rules:
      $$
      \mathbf{m}_l^{(j)}[i] =
      \begin{cases}
      0 & \text{if } |\theta_l^{(j-1)}[i]| \leq \alpha^{(j)} \text{ (global) or } \alpha_l^{(j)} \text{ (local)},\\
      1 & \text{otherwise},
      \end{cases}
      $$
      then set $\theta^{(j)} = \mathbf{m}^{(j)} \odot \theta^{(j-1)}$. Experimentally, the pruning schedule removes 20% of weights per iteration (cumulative up to 80%), applied uniformly to convolutional and MLP layers; training uses Adam with learning rate $1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping patience 10, and experiments are performed on a NVIDIA V4090 GPU. One-shot pruning corresponds to applying $\mathbf{m}^{(1)}$ after one full training cycle.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion describes the specific IMP procedure used; it is a methodological specification not making an empirical claim beyond the algorithm description. No load-bearing weak points or strengths were identified beyond the procedure itself. The configuration (8 rounds, 20% per iteration, Adam lr=1e-4, etc.) is clearly stated and reproducible, but its optimality for deepfake detection is not validated.

nodes.title: Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) procedure and operational configuration for deepfake detection

nodes.content: Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP), and in particular IMP with local (per-layer) thresholds, consistently outperforms one-shot magnitude pruning (pruning all weights in a single step after one full training cycle) across MesoNet, CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet on the OpenForensic and FaceForensics++ datasets. The performance gap increases at sparsity levels above 70%: at 80% sparsity, IMP-Local yields a 1–2 percentage-point accuracy advantage over one-shot pruning on OpenForensic and up to a 2–3 percentage-point advantage on FaceForensics++ across these models. This indicates that iterative refinement better preserves subtle discriminative features needed for deepfake detection.

metadata.narrative: P4 raises that the reported 1–3% advantage of IMP over one-shot lacks statistical quantification and could fall within noise. However, H4 shows that the advantage is completely consistent across 16 comparisons (4 architectures × 2 datasets × 2 sparsity levels), which strongly suggests a systematic effect rather than random variation. The qualitative direction (IMP outperforms one-shot at high sparsity) is moderately supported, but the magnitude (1–3%) is not precisely quantifiable. The comparative ranking layer is credible at a coarse level.

nodes.title: IMP, especially local IMP, consistently outperforms one-shot pruning at high sparsity across architectures and datasets

nodes.content: The effectiveness of global versus local pruning criteria in Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) is dataset-dependent. Global pruning (using a single threshold based on all weights) generalizes better and is more stable on the cleaner, less compressed OpenForensic dataset (140,000 training images, no face cropping). Local pruning (using per-layer thresholds) better preserves accuracy on the challenging, heavily compressed FaceForensics++ dataset (11,600 training images from 400 face-cropped videos with varied compression artifacts). This indicates that dataset statistics and compression artifacts determine which pruning strategy best preserves manipulation-sensitive features.

metadata.narrative: The empirical observation that global pruning works better on OpenForensic and local pruning works better on FaceForensics++ is directly supported by Fig. 2 and constitutes the core of this conclusion. P5 identifies that the causal attribution to compression level is confounded by dataset size, source type (still images vs videos), and preprocessing; therefore, the explanation that "dataset compression artifacts" drive the difference is not isolated. No highlight counterbalances this attribution gap. The empirical claim about dataset-dependent behavior stands, but the explanation and the resulting design guidance (choose pruning strategy based on compression level) are not robustly justified.

nodes.title: Pruning strategy effectiveness is dataset-dependent: global better on OpenForensic, local better on FaceForensics++

nodes.content: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) comparisons between dense (0% sparsity) and pruned (60% and 80% sparsity) ResNet-18 models reveal that pruned subnetworks maintain concentrated attention on semantically meaningful facial regions, notably the cheek and eye areas, even at 80% sparsity, while the attention maps contract and focus on smaller regions. The attention difference is quantified via the Frobenius norm $\Delta L^c(p)=\| L_{\text{original}}^c - L_p^c \|_F$, where $L_{\text{original}}^c$ is the Grad-CAM heatmap for class $c$ from the original dense model and $L_p^c$ is the heatmap from the model at pruning rate $p$. Additionally, qualitative analysis of Grad-CAM heatmaps indicates that pruned networks increasingly emphasize high-frequency artifacts and temporal inconsistencies over broader semantic features as sparsity increases.

metadata.narrative: P6 critically weakens the second half of this conclusion: the claim that pruned networks "increasingly emphasize high-frequency artifacts and temporal inconsistencies" is unsupported—Grad-CAM cannot discriminate frequency bands and the analysis is limited to two single frames. H2 supports the other half: that pruned models maintain focused attention on facial regions (cheek and eyes) with contraction of the high-attention area. The spatial-preservation layer of the conclusion is supported, but the interpretive attribution to specific artifact types is not evidenced. The two halves should be considered separately; only the spatial-preservation claim is validated.

nodes.title: Grad-CAM shows pruned ResNet-18 models preserve attention on facial regions and shift toward high-frequency/temporal artifacts as sparsity increases

nodes.content: Sparse subnetworks (winning tickets) discovered via Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) on the larger OpenForensic dataset transfer effectively to the smaller FaceForensics++ dataset when evaluated directly (zero-shot) with no fine-tuning. At 60% sparsity, an IMP-pruned MesoNet achieves 61.2% accuracy on FaceForensics++, compared to its dense baseline accuracy on FaceForensics++ of 59.9%. At 80% sparsity, an IMP-pruned CNN-5 subnetwork achieves 74.5% accuracy (dense baseline on FaceForensics++: 76.2%) and an IMP-pruned ResNet-18 subnetwork achieves 83.7% accuracy (dense baseline: 85.3%). Thus, subnetworks found on a larger source dataset can be reused on a smaller target dataset with minor accuracy degradation or, in some cases, modest improvement.

metadata.narrative: P7 points out that the transfer experiment uses only zero-shot evaluation (no fine-tuning), limiting the scope of the "transferability" claim to direct reuse without adaptation. H3 strengthens the conclusion by showing that the zero-shot results are consistent across three architectures and two pruning methods, and that IMP subnetworks often match or approach the dense target baselines. The claim of "preserved or improved accuracy" is valid for zero-shot transfer, but the practical implication for full transfer learning (with fine-tuning) is not tested. The conclusion's scope should be understood as zero-shot transfer only.

nodes.title: Sparse subnetworks discovered via IMP on OpenForensic transfer to FaceForensics++ with minor accuracy degradation or modest improvement

nodes.content: Larger, deeper architectures such as ResNet-18 (11.7M parameters) exhibit greater redundancy and stronger lottery-ticket behavior (retaining near-original performance at high sparsity) on both the OpenForensic and FaceForensics++ datasets when pruned using Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP). Compact networks such as MesoNet (0.015M parameters) are more sensitive to pruning and degrade more quickly. This establishes an architecture-dependent trade-off between base model compactness and compressibility: starting with a larger model yields subnetworks that are both small and robust, while very compact models may lack sufficient redundancy to tolerate extreme pruning.

metadata.narrative: P8 shows that the attribution of robustness to "redundancy from larger size" is confounded with architecture design (ResNet-18 has residual connections; MesoNet does not). The empirical ranking (ResNet-18 > CNN-5 > MesoNet at 80% sparsity) is clearly supported by Fig. 2 and by H1. However, the causal explanation—and consequently the design recommendation to "start with a larger model"—is not robustly justified. The conclusion's descriptive layer (which architectures are more robust) is credible; the explanatory/normative layer (why, and which design strategy to adopt) is weakly supported.

nodes.title: ResNet-18 exhibits greater redundancy and stronger lottery-ticket behavior than MesoNet under iterative magnitude pruning

nodes.content: In cross-dataset transfer experiments (zero-shot from OpenForensic to FaceForensics++), subnetworks produced by Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) consistently outperform one-shot-pruned subnetworks at both 60% and 80% sparsity across MesoNet, CNN-5, and ResNet-18. This indicates that iterative pruning produces subnetworks with superior generalization across datasets.

metadata.narrative: P9 highlights that the individual IMP vs one-shot transfer differences (0.4–3.4 percentage points) are single-run estimates and could be within noise. H3 and H4, however, indicate that the pattern of IMP superiority for transfer is consistent across three architectures (MesoNet, CNN-5, ResNet-18) and two sparsity levels, with no counterexample in the data. The qualitative pattern is therefore more robust than any single comparison. The precise magnitude of the advantage remains uncertain. The comparative ranking (IMP yields better transferability) is moderately supported at a coarse level.

nodes.title: IMP yields better transferability than one-shot pruning across architectures and sparsity levels in zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation

nodes.content: In the evaluation of MesoNet on the OpenForensic dataset using iterative magnitude pruning with uniform 20%-per-iteration weight removal across all layers (Conv and MLP), 8 pruning rounds, Adam optimizer with learning rate 1e-4, and early stopping patience 10, the reported test accuracy at 80% sparsity (56.2%) and the dense baseline accuracy (62.6%) are each derived from a single experimental run with no reported standard deviation, confidence interval, or number of random seeds.Fig. 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the true test accuracy at 80% sparsity differed from the reported 56.2% by, say, 4 percentage points (well within single-run noise), then: (1) the absolute performance would be substantially lower (e.g., 52%) or higher (e.g., 60%); (2) the retention ratio relative to the 62.6% dense baseline would shift from 89.8% to 83% or 96%, respectively, weakening or changing the "substantial performance" characterization; (3) the specific quantitative layer of the conclusion (the precise 56.2% and 89.8% figures) would be unsupported. The qualitative direction (that some performance is retained) may still hold, but the claim's quantitative precision is lost.
metadata.weakness_reason: Deep-learning accuracy from a single train–test split and a single parameter initialization can vary by several percentage points due to random weight initialization, data shuffling, and non-deterministic GPU operations. The paper explicitly states that experiments used a single NVIDIA V4090 GPU and does not mention multiple trials, random seeds, or cross-validation anywhere in the text or figures. Without such uncertainty quantification, the reported 56.2% and the derived ratio (89.8% of baseline) cannot be distinguished from values that could be several points lower or higher, making the quantitative claim unverifiable.

nodes.title: Single-run test accuracy for MesoNet at 80% sparsity on OpenForensic

nodes.content: For CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet on the OpenForensic dataset, the reported dense baselines (91.41%, 94.3%, 96.20% respectively) and the 80%-sparsity accuracies (90.88%, 94.29%, 96.11%) are each stated as single-point estimates with no reported variance, number of repetitions, or confidence intervals. For ResNet-18 the dense baseline is given to one decimal place (94.3%) while the sparsity value is given to two (94.29%), producing a 0.01 percentage-point difference that is smaller than typical run-to-run variation in deep learning.Fig. 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the actual sparsity-test accuracy for ResNet-18 were, for example, 93.9% instead of 94.29% (a 0.4% drop, within typical single-run noise), then the retention ratio would change from 99.9% to 99.6%, which still supports the qualitative direction. The more serious failure is that the reported near-perfect retention numbers could be misinterpreted as precise—yet they are not supported by any error analysis. The quantitative layer of the conclusion (the exact retention percentages) is therefore not reliable; the qualitative claim that performance is "near-baseline" is plausible but not rigorously bounded.
metadata.weakness_reason: Single-run classification accuracy for convolutional networks on a fixed test set commonly fluctuates by 0.5–1% due to random initialization, optimizer noise, and data ordering. The 0.01% difference between ResNet-18's dense and sparse reported values is well below this noise floor. The precision mismatch (one decimal vs two) further suggests rounding that masks the actual variability. Without multiple seeds or cross-validation, the claim that each architecture "maintains near-baseline accuracy at 99.4%–99.9% retention" is not statistically distinct from a claim of 98% or 100.1% retention.

nodes.title: Single-run accuracy for CNN-5/ResNet-18/XceptionNet at 80% sparsity on OpenForensic

nodes.content: ResNet-18 pruned with iterative magnitude pruning using local thresholds yields 83% accuracy at 80% sparsity on FaceForensics++, which is claimed to outperform both the dense baseline and IMP-Global. However, the dense baseline accuracy for ResNet-18 on FaceForensics++ is 85.3%, which is higher than 83%, meaning the 80%-sparsity subnetwork does not outperform the dense baseline.Fig. 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the claim of outperforming the baseline is false (as the numbers suggest), then the core comparative ranking of the conclusion—that local pruning at 80% sparsity yields "superior" performance relative to the dense model on FaceForensics++—is invalidated. The remaining subclaims (local outperforms global) may still hold, but the conclusion as written asserts a ranking (local ≥ dense) that is unsupported. The scope of damage: the comparative layer of the conclusion is fully invalidated.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper provides two sources of data: Fig. 2 shows the 83% value at 80% sparsity (IMP-Local), and Table I gives the dense baseline for ResNet-18 on FaceForensics++ as 85.3%. Comparing 83% against 85.3% directly contradicts the claim that the pruned model outperforms the overparameterized baseline. No other baseline or alternative interpretation is offered to resolve this contradiction; the conclusion is therefore self-contradicting.

nodes.title: Internal contradiction: ResNet-18 local pruning accuracy (83%) is below dense baseline (85.3%) on FaceForensics++

nodes.content: Across all architectures and both datasets, the reported advantage of iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) over one-shot pruning ranges from 1–3 percentage points (1–2% on OpenForensic, up to 2–3% on FaceForensics++). None of these differences are accompanied by standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed comparisons; single-run accuracy values are reported for each method.Fig. 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the true mean accuracy of IMP and one-shot pruning were equal (i.e., no systematic advantage), then the conclusion that IMP "consistently outperforms" one-shot would be false. Even if the true advantage were positive but smaller than reported, the specific edge (1–2% on OpenForensic, 2–3% on FaceForensics++) would be unreliable. The scope of damage: the comparative ranking and the quantitative magnitude are both unsubstantiated.
metadata.weakness_reason: In deep-learning benchmarking, single-run classification accuracy on a fixed test set can vary by 0.5–1% due to initialization and data ordering. The reported advantage of 1–3% falls in a range where such variation could reverse the ranking for individual comparisons. Without multiple trials or a statistical test, the claim that "IMP consistently outperforms one-shot pruning" is not quantitatively robust.

nodes.title: No statistical quantification for IMP vs one-shot advantage

nodes.content: The conclusion that global pruning is more effective on cleaner, less compressed data (OpenForensic) while local pruning is better on heavily compressed data (FaceForensics++) is based on only two datasets that differ in multiple aspects besides compression level: dataset size (140,000 vs 11,600 training images), data source (still images vs videos), preprocessing (no face-cropping vs face-cropping), and manipulation types (single curated set vs varied generation methods). The effect of compression level is not experimentally isolated from these confounds.Fig. 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the true cause of the pruning-strategy preference is dataset size or video domain rather than compression, then the paper's recommendation to choose pruning strategy based on compression level would be unfounded. For example, a heavily compressed but large still-image dataset might behave like OpenForensic (favoring global pruning), contradicting the compression-based rule. The scope of damage: the explanatory/attribution layer of the conclusion is invalidated; the empirical observation that the two datasets differ remains, but the practical guidance is not justified.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper attributes the different performance patterns to "compression artifacts" and "cleaner" vs "challenging" data. However, the two datasets differ on many uncontrolled dimensions: OpenForensic is a large collection of still images, FaceForensics++ is a smaller set of face-cropped video frames with multiple compression types. The observed reversal of global vs local pruning effectiveness could be due to dataset size (larger datasets may favor global pruning), the presence of video-specific temporal artifacts, or the face-cropping preprocessing, rather than compression level per se.

nodes.title: Confounded attribution of pruning strategy effectiveness to compression level

nodes.content: The claim that as sparsity increases pruned networks increasingly emphasize high-frequency artifacts and temporal inconsistencies over broader semantic features is based on qualitative visual inspection of Grad-CAM heatmaps on two example images (one fake, one real). Grad-CAM produces spatial attention maps over pixel coordinates and does not directly discriminate between frequency bands (high vs low frequency) or capture temporal information (it operates on single frames).Fig. 3

metadata.failure_mode: If the claim about high-frequency/temporal emphasis is unsupported, then the paper's interpretation of how pruning changes feature reliance is speculative and not evidenced. The conclusion that pruning shifts reliance to these specific artifact types fails; the only observation that remains supported is that attention regions contract and remain on facial areas (which Grad-CAM can show). The scope of damage: the interpretive attribution layer of the conclusion is fully invalidated.
metadata.weakness_reason: Grad-CAM highlights input regions that contribute to the network's class prediction based on gradient flow through a convolutional layer. The resulting heatmap can reflect texture, shape, or edge cues, but it cannot by itself indicate that the attended regions correspond specifically to high-frequency artifacts (e.g., pixel-level discontinuities) rather than lower-frequency facial features. To support a claim about frequency content, the paper would need additional frequency-domain analysis (e.g., Fourier transform of the attended regions, or high-pass filtering). Similarly, "temporal inconsistencies" would require frame-difference or video-level analysis, which is absent. Furthermore, the claim is based on only two images, offering no statistical basis for generalization.

nodes.title: Grad-CAM cannot directly support claim of high-frequency or temporal artifact emphasis

nodes.content: Transferability is evaluated by taking a sparse subnetwork trained on the OpenForensic dataset (source) and testing it directly on the FaceForensics++ dataset (target) with no fine-tuning, adaptation, or retraining on the target data. Transferability is defined as $a_2' \approx a_2$, where $\theta_2 = \mathbf{m}_1 \odot \theta_1$, with $a_2'$ the accuracy of the sparse network on the target dataset and $a_2$ the accuracy of the original dense network. In practical transfer learning, models are typically fine-tuned on the target domain; this evaluation does not test whether fine-tuning would improve, degrade, or leave performance unchanged.Table I

metadata.failure_mode: If the transferred subnetworks were subsequently fine-tuned and performed worse than the zero-shot result (e.g., due to catastrophic forgetting or distribution mismatch), then the claim of effective transferability would need to be reassessed. Even without that scenario, the phrasing "sparse subnetworks transfer ... with preserved or improved accuracy" implies a level of practical reuse that the zero-shot-only evaluation does not fully support. The scope of damage: the generalization layer of the conclusion is limited to zero-shot transfer; the practical recommendation to reuse winning tickets across datasets without adaptation is not validated.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's experimental design measures only zero-shot transfer—how well a subnetwork trained on one dataset performs on a different dataset without any further training. While this is a valid scientific measurement, it does not correspond to typical deployment scenarios where practitioners would fine-tune the transferred model on the target dataset. Moreover, the reported cases where the zero-shot subnetwork outperforms the dense baseline trained on the target (e.g., MesoNet at 60% sparsity: 61.2% vs dense 59.9%) are interesting but unexplained; they could reflect that the source dataset provides better feature learning or that the dense baseline on the small target dataset is undertrained. The conclusion's scope is therefore limited to zero-shot transfer, which the text does not explicitly restrict.

nodes.title: Transfer experiment uses zero-shot evaluation without fine-tuning

nodes.content: The conclusion that larger, deeper architectures (ResNet-18, 11.7M parameters) exhibit greater redundancy and stronger lottery-ticket behavior, while compact networks (MesoNet, 0.015M) are more brittle, attributes the difference to redundancy that scales with model size. However, ResNet-18 and MesoNet differ not only in parameter count but also in architectural features: ResNet-18 uses residual skip connections while MesoNet uses a sequence of plain convolutional and fully-connected layers. These design differences are known to affect pruning robustness independently of size.Fig. 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the robustness of ResNet-18 owes primarily to its residual connections rather than its larger parameter count, then the design recommendation to "start with a larger model" (conclusion 9) would be misleading: a larger non-residual model might still be brittle, while a smaller residual model might be robust. The causal attribution of the conclusion would be invalidated, although the empirical ranking (ResNet-18 > MesoNet at 80% sparsity) remains correct. The scope of damage: the explanatory and design-recommendation layers of the conclusion are weakened.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper treats architecture size as the primary factor explaining pruning robustness, but the comparison confounds size with other design choices. Residual connections in ResNet-18 explicitly preserve gradient flow and facilitate feature reuse, which are known to help pruning robustness (e.g., the lottery ticket hypothesis is more often demonstrated in residual architectures). MesoNet's shallow, non-residual design may make it inherently less robust regardless of size. The paper does not decompose these factors, so the attribution to "redundancy" (i.e., number of parameters) is not isolated.

nodes.title: Attribution of robustness to 'redundancy from larger size' confounded with architectural design

nodes.content: In the transfer experiment, IMP consistently outperforms one-shot pruning across three architectures (MesoNet, CNN-5, ResNet-18) at both 60% and 80% sparsity, with the advantage ranging from 0.4 to 3.4 percentage points. However, all reported values are single-run estimates with no error bars, standard deviations, or multiple-seed repetitions.Table I

metadata.failure_mode: If the true transfer accuracies of IMP and one-shot are equal (i.e., no systematic advantage), then the conclusion that IMP yields "better transferability" is false. Even if a true advantage exists but is smaller than reported, the conclusion's quantitative claim of superior transfer would be misleading. The scope of damage: the comparative ranking is unsubstantiated.
metadata.weakness_reason: Standard deep-learning practice requires multiple random seeds to distinguish systematic differences from noise. The reported advantages (e.g., 0.4% for ResNet-18 at 60% sparsity) are within the typical variation of a single run. Without uncertainty quantification, the claim that "IMP yields better transferability than one-shot pruning" cannot be statistically grounded; the observed pattern could reverse in a different run.

nodes.title: No statistical quantification for IMP vs one-shot transfer advantage

nodes.content: The evaluation spans four neural architectures (MesoNet, CNN-5, ResNet-18, XceptionNet) and two datasets (OpenForensic with 140,000 training images, FaceForensics++ with 11,600 training images, face-cropped from 400 videos) under a single, explicitly specified training and pruning protocol: Adam optimizer with learning rate 1e-4, early stopping patience 10, 8 pruning rounds with uniform 20% per-iteration weight removal, and two thresholding strategies (global and local) consistently applied across all conditions.

metadata.credit: This systematic multi-architecture, multi-dataset design preempts the failure mode where observed pruning behavior could be idiosyncratic to a single architecture or dataset (e.g., only seen in one network type or on one data distribution). Because the same protocol is applied across all conditions, the conclusions—that certain architectures preserve performance at 80% sparsity, that IMP outperforms one-shot, and that pruning-strategy effectiveness depends on the dataset—are demonstrated to hold across a diverse range of network designs and data characteristics. Without this scope, each conclusion would be vulnerable to the criticism that it only applies to a narrow setup. The credit underwrites the generalization layer of conclusions 1–3, 5, 6, and 9.

nodes.title: Multi-architecture, multi-dataset evaluation under consistent protocol

nodes.content: Grad-CAM heatmaps from a ResNet-18 model are provided at sparsity levels 0% (dense), 60%, and 80% for both a deepfake and a real facial image, showing that the highlighted regions (red areas of highest activation) remain concentrated on the cheek and eye areas with increasing sparsity, and that the spatial extent of high-attention regions contracts as sparsity increases.

metadata.credit: The comparison of heatmaps across three sparsity levels provides visual evidence that pruned models do not divert attention to irrelevant background regions; instead they maintain focus on semantically meaningful facial features. This preempts the failure mode where pruning might have been found to cause attention to become random or shift to non-discriminative regions, which would undermine the interpretability of pruned deepfake detectors. The credit is that the spatial-preservation layer of conclusion 7 (focused attention on facial regions) is visually supported, though the claim about high-frequency/temporal artifacts is not covered by this strength.

nodes.title: Grad-CAM visualizations show consistent spatial attention at three sparsity levels

nodes.content: The transfer experiment evaluates three architectures (MesoNet, CNN-5, ResNet-18) at two sparsity levels (60% and 80%) and compares both IMP and one-shot pruned subnetworks (trained on OpenForensic, tested on FaceForensics++) against dense baselines trained on the target dataset (FaceForensics++), all reported in a single table (Table I).

metadata.credit: This multi-architecture, multi-sparsity, two-method design preempts the failure mode where transferability could be claimed on the basis of a single architecture or pruning method. By including dense baselines trained on the target dataset, the experiment provides a concrete benchmark against which the transferred subnetworks are measured, allowing readers to assess the cost of zero-shot transfer. The consistent pattern across architectures (IMP at 60% sparsity matching or exceeding the dense baseline) strengthens the conclusion that winning tickets discovered on a larger dataset can be reused on a smaller dataset with competitive accuracy. The credit underwrites the generalization layer of conclusion 8 (transferability) and of conclusion 10 (IMP superior for transfer).

nodes.title: Systematic cross-dataset transfer evaluation with head-to-head baselines

nodes.content: In 16 distinct comparisons (four architectures × two datasets × two sparsity levels) reported in Fig. 2 and Table I, iterative magnitude pruning (IMP, either global or local) achieves higher test accuracy than one-shot pruning at high sparsity (≥60%), with the advantage most pronounced on FaceForensics++ (up to 2–3%). The pattern holds without exception across all reported conditions.

metadata.credit: The complete consistency of the IMP advantage across 16 comparisons—covering multiple architectures, two datasets, and two sparsity levels—preempts the failure mode where the advantage could be coincidental in a single setting. Even though individual comparisons lack error bars, the fact that no counterexample exists among all reported experiments raises the likelihood that the advantage is systematic rather than due to chance. This underwrites the comparative ranking layer of conclusion 5 (IMP outperforms one-shot at high sparsity).

nodes.title: Consistent IMP advantage over one-shot pruning across architectures and datasets

steps.reasoning:
Start from the established IMP operational configuration and experimental protocol: use the iterative pruning schedule with $J=8$ rounds, uniform 20% removal per round to reach 80% sparsity, training with Adam at learning rate $1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping patience 10, and experiments executed on NVIDIA V4090. Treat these IMP settings as known inputs to the experimental outcome.
[6]

Describe the data context for this result: the OpenForensic dataset used for these experiments contains 140,000 images for training and 11,000 images for testing, and the MesoNet architecture is a lightweight network designed to capture mesoscopic manipulation artifacts, as specified in the dataset and architecture descriptions.
[11]

Report the experimental observation for MesoNet under the IMP-Global procedure on OpenForensic: after applying iterative magnitude pruning to 80% global sparsity, MesoNet achieves test accuracy of $56.2\%$ on the OpenForensic test set. This numeric value is the empirical measurement reported in the study for MesoNet at 80% sparsity on OpenForensic.
Fig. 2

Provide the dense baseline for comparison: the dense (0% sparsity) MesoNet baseline accuracy on OpenForensic is $62.6\%$, as reported in the same experimental results, and the 80%-sparse accuracy is compared against this baseline to compute relative retention.
Fig. 2

Compute the relative retention percentage explicitly: compute $\dfrac{56.2}{62.6}\times 100\% \approx 89.8\%$, showing that the 80%-sparse MesoNet retains approximately $89.8\%$ of the dense-model accuracy on OpenForensic. This arithmetic follows directly from the two reported accuracies.

Provide the parameter-count evidence: the 80% sparse MesoNet has approximately $0.003$ million parameters (i.e., about $3{,}000$ parameters), as reported in the transferability Table I parameter column for 80% pruning of MesoNet. This supports the claim about the compressed subnetwork size.
Table I

Conclude from the empirical measurements that a highly compressed MesoNet subnetwork discovered via iterative magnitude pruning preserves most of the original detection performance on OpenForensic: combining the numeric accuracy ($56.2\%$), the baseline ($62.6\%$), their ratio ($\approx89.8\%$), and the parameter count ($\approx3{,}000$) yields the stated conclusion about preservation of detection performance under extreme compression.
Fig. 2

Start from the IMP experimental configuration used for OpenForensic: iterative magnitude pruning with 8 rounds, 20% weight removal per iteration (cumulative to 80% sparsity), training with Adam at learning rate $1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping patience 10. Treat this configuration as the experimental basis.
[6]

State the OpenForensic baseline accuracies for the three evaluated architectures as reported in the results: CNN-5 dense baseline accuracy is $91.41\%$, ResNet-18 dense baseline accuracy is $94.30\%$, and XceptionNet dense baseline accuracy is $96.20\%$. These baselines are the references used to compute relative retention after pruning.
Fig. 2

Report the measured 80%-sparsity accuracies under IMP-Global on OpenForensic: CNN-5 achieves $90.88\%$, ResNet-18 achieves $94.29\%$, and XceptionNet achieves $96.11\%$ at 80% sparsity, as stated in the empirical findings for OpenForensic.
Fig. 2

Compute and present the retention ratios explicitly: for CNN-5 compute $\dfrac{90.88}{91.41}\times100\%\approx99.4\%$; for ResNet-18 compute $\dfrac{94.29}{94.30}\times100\%\approx99.9\%$; for XceptionNet compute $\dfrac{96.11}{96.20}\times100\%\approx99.9\%$. These arithmetic computations follow directly from the reported sparse and dense accuracies.

Synthesize the implication: because the three architectures retain approximately $99\%$ or higher of their dense-model accuracies at 80% sparsity under IMP-Global on OpenForensic, conclude that large and medium architectures contain sparse subnetworks that preserve nearly all original performance at extreme sparsity in this dataset setting.
Fig. 2

Begin from the IMP methodology and the distinction between global and local pruning thresholds established in the IMP procedure: local pruning applies a per-layer threshold $\alpha_l^{(j)}$ for iteration $j$, enabling layer-wise control over which weights are pruned while global pruning uses a single $\alpha^{(j)}$ across all layers.

Describe the dataset and its characteristics relevant to this result: the combined FaceForensics++ dataset (augmented with Celeb-DF as used by the authors) comprises heavily compressed and varied deepfake generation artifacts; in the experimental setup, 40 face-cropped frames per video yielded 11,600 images for training and 2,400 for evaluation, representing a more challenging, compressed-data regime than OpenForensic.
[12]

Report the empirical observation for ResNet-18 under local pruning on FaceForensics++: applying iterative magnitude pruning with local (per-layer) thresholds and following the 8-round, 20% per-round schedule yields $83\%$ accuracy at 80% sparsity for ResNet-18 on FaceForensics++, as stated in the experimental results.
Fig. 2

Compare this 80%-sparse local-pruned accuracy against the two baselines noted in the study: (a) the overparameterized dense baseline (ResNet-18 at 0% pruning) and (b) the same ResNet-18 pruned with the global thresholding strategy (IMP-Global). The authors report that under the FaceForensics++ regime, the 80%-sparse IMP-Local ResNet-18 outperforms both the overparameterized baseline and the IMP-Global variant, i.e., local pruning yields the highest accuracy among these options in this setting.
Fig. 2

Conclude the mechanistic implication emphasized by the authors: because local (per-layer) pruning preserves $83\%$ accuracy at 80% sparsity and surpasses both global pruning and the dense baseline in this compressed, artifact-rich dataset, local pruning better preserves critical layer-specific features that are important for detection under heavy compression and varied generation artifacts.

Define the neural network considered: let $\mathcal{F}(\mathrm{x};\theta)$ denote a neural network that maps input images $\mathrm{x}\in\mathcal{X}$ to binary labels in $\mathcal{Y}$, where the network parameters are $\theta$ initialized from distribution $\mathcal{D}_{\theta}$. Define a binary mask $\mathbf{m}\in\{0,1\}^{|\theta|}$ that will select the subnetwork. These symbol definitions are used throughout the IMP specification.
Specify mask initialization: set the initial mask to all ones, $\mathbf{m}^{(0)}=\mathbf{1}$, meaning no weights are pruned at the start. This is the starting point for the iterative procedure.

Describe training-with-mask operation: at iteration $j$ train the masked network $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{m}^{(j-1)}\odot\theta^{(j-1)})$, where $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication between mask and weights, and $\theta^{(j-1)}$ are the weights after the previous pruning update.

Define pruning thresholding and mask update rules precisely for both global and local criteria: for layer index $l$ and weight index $i$ the updated mask entry $\mathbf{m}_l^{(j)}[i]$ is
$$
\mathbf{m}_l^{(j)}[i] =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } |\theta_l^{(j-1)}[i]| \leq \alpha^{(j)} \text{ (global) or } \alpha_l^{(j)} \text{ (local)},\\
1 & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
$$
where $\alpha^{(j)}$ is a global threshold computed from the distribution of all weights, and $\alpha_l^{(j)}$ is a per-layer threshold computed from the distribution of weights in layer $l$.

State weight update after pruning: after computing the new mask, update the stored weights by applying the mask: $\theta^{(j)}=\mathbf{m}^{(j)}\odot\theta^{(j-1)}$. This concretely removes the pruned weights from subsequent training.

Operationalize the iterative schedule used in experiments: perform $J=8$ pruning rounds (i.e., $j=1,\dots,J$), where in each pruning round the network is trained for one training cycle and then 20% of the remaining weights are removed (uniform 20% weight removal per iteration), yielding cumulative sparsities up to 80% after the eight rounds. State that both convolutional (Conv) layers and multilayer perceptron (MLP) layers are treated uniformly with respect to this 20% per-iteration removal.

Define one-shot pruning in contrast: one-shot pruning corresponds to training for a single full training cycle and then applying the mask update $\mathbf{m}^{(1)}$ once to reach the desired sparsity (i.e., apply the thresholding rule once instead of iteratively).

Provide the experimental training hyperparameters and runtime context used in the study: training uses the Adam optimizer with learning rate $1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping with patience 10, and the experiments were run on a single NVIDIA V4090 GPU. These settings were applied to every IMP iteration and to the one-shot baseline as described.

Summarize the algorithmic pseudocode and reference its role: Algorithm 1 implements the above loop—initialize $\theta$ and $m\leftarrow 1$, for $j=1,\dots,J$ train $F(x;m\odot\theta)$ for $T$ epochs, compute the pruning threshold(s) $\alpha^{(j)}$ or $\alpha_l^{(j)}$, set $m_l[i]\leftarrow 0$ when $|\theta_l[i]|\leq\alpha^{(j)}$ (or $\alpha_l^{(j)}$), and finally set $\theta\leftarrow m\odot\theta$ before the next round—thereby operationalizing IMP for the deepfake detection experiments.
[6]

Begin from the IMP experimental protocol and its one-shot baseline: experiments compared Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with both global and local thresholds against a one-shot magnitude-pruning baseline where the mask $\mathbf{m}^{(1)}$ is applied after a single training cycle.

Report the aggregate empirical pattern observed across architectures and datasets: IMP, and particularly IMP with local per-layer thresholds (IMP-Local), consistently outperforms one-shot pruning across the evaluated models and datasets, with the advantage increasing at high sparsity levels (greater than $70\%$).
Fig. 2

Quantify the reported performance gaps at 80% sparsity: on OpenForensic IMP-Local yields a $1$--$2\%$ test accuracy advantage over one-shot pruning for all models, and on FaceForensics++ IMP-Local yields up to a $2$--$3\%$ accuracy advantage versus one-shot across models. These numeric gaps are the empirical observations stated in the results.

Explain the authors' interpretation of why iterative pruning outperforms one-shot: iterative refinement via IMP allows the mask and weights to co-adapt across multiple training-and-prune cycles, which better preserves subtle discriminative features than a single-shot removal that may prematurely eliminate weights linked to rare or fragile features.
[21]

Conclude that IMP, and especially IMP-Local, is the superior pruning strategy in the evaluated deepfake-detection experiments for maintaining accuracy at extreme sparsity because it repeatedly trains and prunes, allowing retention of critical discriminative weights that one-shot pruning tends to remove.

Start from the empirical comparisons between IMP-Global and IMP-Local reported in the study: on OpenForensic (a cleaner, less-compressed image dataset) IMP-Global outperformed IMP-Local across the evaluated models, while on the more heavily-compressed FaceForensics++ dataset IMP-Local outperformed IMP-Global and even the overparameterized baseline.
Fig. 2

Characterize dataset-specific properties influencing pruning effectiveness: OpenForensic is described as cleaner and less compressed (140,000 training images, 11,000 test images), whereas FaceForensics++ contains compression and temporal/manipulation artifacts (40 frames per video, 11,600 frames for training, 2,400 for evaluation), making it a more challenging and artifact-rich domain for deepfake detection.
[11]
[12]

Explain the observed mechanism linking dataset statistics to pruning criterion success: in the cleaner OpenForensic case, global pruning (which ranks weights by magnitude across the entire network) generalizes better and yields more stable importance estimates, preserving performance. In contrast, in the compressed, artifact-rich FaceForensics++ case, layer-wise (local) thresholds preserve layer-specific, potentially rare features tied to compression artifacts, which global pruning might remove.

State the authors' synthesis into a dataset-dependent recommendation: the choice between global and local pruning should be informed by dataset characteristics—prefer global pruning for cleaner datasets where overall weight importance suffices, and prefer local pruning for heavily compressed or artifact-rich datasets where preserving layer-specific patterns is critical for maintaining manipulation-sensitive features.

Define the Grad-CAM analysis formalism used: for convolutional layer $l$ let $A^l$ denote the feature map activations, and for class $c$ compute importance weights $\alpha_k^c$ from the gradients of the class score $y^c$ with respect to $A^l$. The Grad-CAM heatmap is formed as
$$
L^c = \text{ReLU}\!\left(\sum_k \alpha_k^c A^k\right),
$$
where $\text{ReLU}$ denotes the rectified linear unit and $k$ indexes feature maps; this equation specifies how class-specific importance is aggregated into a spatial heatmap.
[22]

Define the quantitative metric used to measure attention change across pruning levels: for class $c$ and pruning rate $p$ let $L_{\text{original}}^c$ be the heatmap before pruning and $L_p^c$ the heatmap at pruning rate $p$; the authors quantify attention difference as
$$
\Delta L^c(p)=\| L_{\text{original}}^c - L_p^c \|_F,
$$
where $\|\cdot\|_F$ denotes the Frobenius norm. This provides a numeric measure of how much attention maps change with pruning.

Report the qualitative and localization findings from empirical Grad-CAM comparisons across sparsity levels 0%, 60%, and 80%: the activation maps remain concentrated on semantically meaningful facial regions—particularly the cheek and eye areas—even at 80% sparsity, but the highlighted regions contract and concentrate on smaller, more localized areas as sparsity increases; the highest-activation regions (red in the visualizations) remain positioned in similar facial areas across sparsity levels, indicating preserved attention to relevant regions despite pruning.
Fig. 3

Report the additional qualitative observation about feature emphasis shift with increased sparsity: the authors note that pruned networks increasingly emphasize high-frequency artifacts and temporal inconsistencies over broader semantic features as sparsity increases, i.e., the pruned models appear to rely more on fine-grained artifact cues and temporal irregularities than on extensive semantic facial regions.
Fig. 3

Synthesize the combined quantitative and qualitative interpretation: because $\Delta L^c(p)$ remains small enough to show conserved focus on key facial regions while the spatial extent of activations shrinks, and because qualitative inspection indicates a shift toward artifact/high-frequency/temporal cues at higher sparsities, conclude that pruned subnetworks preserve concentrated attention on meaningful facial regions while increasingly relying on finer artifact signals as model capacity is reduced.

Begin from the transferability formalism: given two datasets $\mathcal{D}_1$ (source) and $\mathcal{D}_2$ (target), and a sparse subnetwork $\mathcal{F}_1(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{m}_1\odot\theta_1)$ discovered on $\mathcal{D}_1$, transferability is measured by applying the same mask to the target initialization, $\theta_2=\mathbf{m}_1\odot\theta_1$, and evaluating target accuracy $a_2'$ relative to the dense target accuracy $a_2$; the paper defines transferability as $a_2'\approx a_2$.

State the experimental transfer setting used: the authors discover sparse subnetworks on the larger OpenForensic dataset and then transfer those masks and pruned weights to the smaller FaceForensics++ dataset (the target), evaluating accuracy on the target dataset using the transferred subnetworks; Table I summarizes these cross-dataset transfer results.
Table I

Provide explicit numerical transfer results from Table I for MesoNet at 60% sparsity: the dense MesoNet baseline on FaceForensics++ is $59.9\%$; transferring an IMP-pruned MesoNet at 60% sparsity yields $61.2\%$ accuracy on FaceForensics++, while one-shot transfer yields $59.8\%$. These reported numbers show that the IMP-discovered sparse subnetwork slightly improves target accuracy relative to the dense baseline.
Table I

Provide explicit numerical transfer results for CNN-5 and ResNet-18 at 80% sparsity from Table I: for CNN-5 an 80% IMP subnetwork yields $74.5\%$ on FaceForensics++ versus the dense baseline $76.2\%$ (a modest degradation), and for ResNet-18 an 80% IMP subnetwork yields $83.7\%$ versus the dense baseline $85.3\%$. These numbers indicate that transferred subnetworks remain competitive with the dense baselines at extreme sparsity.
Table I

Interpret the empirical pattern: because IMP-derived subnetworks discovered on the larger OpenForensic dataset—when transferred to the smaller FaceForensics++ dataset—yield either minor accuracy degradation or small improvements (e.g., MesoNet 60% IMP: $61.2\%$ vs dense $59.9\%$), conclude that winning tickets found on a larger source dataset can be reused on a smaller target dataset with preserved or sometimes improved accuracy.

Start from the reported architecture-specific performance curves and comparisons: the study reports per-architecture behavior under IMP pruning across sparsity levels and datasets, summarized in the performance figures and narrative.
Fig. 2

Present ResNet-18 empirical behavior: ResNet-18 consistently retains near-original performance up to 80% sparsity on both OpenForensic and FaceForensics++; for example, on OpenForensic ResNet-18 retains $94.29\%$ at 80% sparsity versus $94.30\%$ dense, indicating strong redundancy and robustness to pruning.
Fig. 2

Present MesoNet empirical behavior: MesoNet, a compact model, shows stronger sensitivity to pruning—on OpenForensic its accuracy drops from $62.6\%$ dense to $56.2\%$ at 80% sparsity, and the authors note that its performance degrades more rapidly beyond the 80% threshold—indicating brittleness under extreme compression.
Fig. 2

Synthesize the architectural inference: because the deeper/wider ResNet-18 preserves performance at extreme sparsity while the compact MesoNet degrades more quickly, conclude that larger architectures possess greater redundancy and stronger lottery-ticket behavior (i.e., they contain small, high-performing subnetworks), whereas very compact models lack sufficient redundancy and are more brittle to extreme pruning.

State the practical trade-off highlighted by the authors: starting from a larger model can yield subnetworks that are both small and robust after pruning, whereas beginning from a very compact model produces less compressibility and more rapid performance degradation, establishing an architecture-dependent trade-off between base model compactness and compressibility.

Begin from the transfer experiments and comparative evaluations reported in the study: the authors compare subnetworks discovered with IMP against subnetworks obtained by one-shot pruning when transferred from OpenForensic to FaceForensics++, and present quantitative results in Table I.
Table I

Extract the comparative numbers from Table I showing IMP surpassing one-shot after transfer: e.g., for MesoNet at 60% sparsity IMP yields $61.2\%$ while one-shot yields $59.8\%$ on FaceForensics++; for CNN-5 at 60% sparsity IMP yields $76.1\%$ vs one-shot $75.5\%$; for ResNet-18 at 60% sparsity IMP yields $85.6\%$ vs one-shot $84.9\%$. These numerical comparisons demonstrate IMP's advantage in transfer settings.
Table I

Note the consistency of the pattern across pruning rates: Table I also shows IMP results exceeding one-shot results at 80% pruning for the same models (e.g., MesoNet 80% IMP $59.3\%$ vs one-shot $55.9\%$; CNN-5 80% IMP $74.5\%$ vs one-shot $73.3\%$; ResNet-18 80% IMP $83.7\%$ vs one-shot $83.3\%$), indicating that IMP produces subnetworks with superior cross-dataset generalization at both 60% and 80% sparsity levels.
Table I

Interpret the mechanism: iterative pruning (IMP) enables mask and weight co-adaptation across multiple training-and-prune cycles, which better preserves features that generalize across datasets relative to a one-shot mask computed after a single training cycle; this methodological difference explains why IMP-produced subnetworks transfer with higher accuracy.

Conclude from the empirical evidence that IMP yields better-transfer subnetworks than one-shot pruning across the evaluated models and pruning rates, as summarized by the consistent superiority of IMP results over one-shot results in the transfer table.

open_questions.content: The authors explicitly acknowledge several unresolved scientific and practical issues left open by this work that merit future investigation. First, the experiments operate at frame level for video datasets (FaceForensics++), so temporal dynamics intrinsic to video deepfakes are not fully captured; developing temporal-aware pruning strategies and evaluating winning tickets in temporally informed architectures remains open. Second, the pruning criteria used (magnitude-based global and local thresholds with fixed 20% per-iteration removal) were not specifically optimized to preserve manipulation artifacts; understanding how alternative pruning signals (e.g., gradient-based saliency, feature-frequency importance, or artifact-aware importance measures) affect rare-feature preservation is unresolved. Third, the IMP procedure incurs substantial computational overhead (eight iterative rounds with retraining), limiting real-time applicability; designing efficient retraining or winning-ticket discovery strategies that reduce computational cost is an open engineering challenge. Fourth, the sensitivity of winning-ticket discovery to pruning granularity (smaller steps such as 5–10% per iteration) and to alternative one-shot selection methods (SNIP, GraSP, layer-wise saliency) remains unquantified for deepfake detection tasks. Fifth, the relationship between network sparsity and robustness to adversarial attacks, and the transferability of winning tickets across different deepfake generation methods (beyond the datasets evaluated), are open scientific questions. Collectively, these limitations define concrete directions: (a) develop temporal- and artifact-aware pruning methods, (b) evaluate alternate pruning criteria and finer-grained schedules for preserving rare manipulation features, (c) devise lower-cost procedures for identifying transferable winning tickets, and (d) systematically study sparsity versus adversarial robustness and generalization across generation families.
